**Owner**
- `src/features/settings/` (proposed) owns the capability.
- It owns the saved settings data (server, via one query cache entry) and the editable draft. The draft is local state with explicit reset and commit, never a second server authority.

**Placement**
- `src/features/settings/index.ts` (proposed) is the public entry. It exports the `SettingsPage` component and the types.
- `src/features/settings/settings.api.ts` (proposed) is the single API owner for read and save. It follows the existing `src/features/cart/cart.api.ts` pattern.
- `src/features/settings/model.ts` (proposed) holds the types and the draft and commit logic, following `src/features/cart/model.ts`.
- `src/features/settings/components/` (proposed) holds `ProfileTab`, `NotificationsTab` and `BillingTab`, plus a shared form provider or hook. The tabs are used only by this capability, so they stay private. No `_shared/` is needed unless a piece is used by several tabs and grows.
- `src/app/settings/page.tsx` (proposed) is the route. It is only composition: it imports `SettingsPage` from `@/features/settings` and nothing deeper.
- Tab selection belongs in the URL (a search param or nested segment). The URL is its own owner, so don't mirror it in state.
- Nothing goes into `src/shared/`. There is no second unrelated consumer, and the form is domain-aware.

**Edge note**
- **Operations:** read settings, and save settings (one mutation covering all three tabs).

- **Invalidation:** invalidate or refetch on save success.

**Recommendation: don't migrate the whole SPA to Next.js. Give the marketing pages static or prerendered HTML and keep the SPA for the app.** This is advisory only. I haven't opened the repo, so every fact below is `assumed` and no files were written.

## 1. Reversibility
This is a **one-way door**. Moving to Next.js changes the rendering strategy, routing, data-fetching, auth and session handling, and hosting runtime for every route. Undoing it means redoing all of those. The migration cost is the verdict, not the word "architecture".

## 2. Problem and constraints
- **Problem (known):** marketing pages need indexable HTML. A client-rendered SPA gives crawlers an empty shell and gives link previews no per-page meta tags.
- **Constraints (all assumed):** a small team of 2-4 React engineers, with no hard deadline.
  - The app routes are authenticated, with no SEO need and no offline mode.
  - Marketing is about 5-20 pages that change at deploy time or through a CMS.
  - The SPA is currently hosted as static files with rewrites.

## 3. Options
- **A. Keep the SPA and make only the marketing routes static or prerendered.** Either prerender at build time, or serve a separate static marketing site on the same domain.
- **B. Migrate the whole app to Next.js.**
- **C. Defer and rely on Google rendering the JavaScript.** This fails the gate if social previews or ranking matter.

## 4. Scores (1 = poor, 3 = strong)

| Criterion | A: static marketing, SPA stays | B: full Next.js | C: defer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fit | 3 — static HTML solves the stated problem | 3 — covers it, plus unneeded SSR | 1 — fails the SEO gate if the requirement is hard (assumed) |
| Cost | 3 — est. 2-5 team-days (assumed) | 1 — est. 15-40 team-days for routing, data, auth and hosting (assumed) | 3 — none now |
| Reversibility | 3 — additive, and marketing can move to Next.js later | 1 — expensive exit | 3 — nothing committed |
| Coupling | 3 — the app stays framework-neutral | 1 — adds a server runtime and Next conventions | 3 — none |
| Failure mode | 2 — a second build to keep in sync, and style drift | 2 — the Next layer grows into a second backend | 1 — pages go unindexed |
| Team fit | 3 — existing stack | 2 — new runtime to operate | 3 — no change |

- **Gate:** C fails if SEO is a hard requirement, so it is out.
- **A over B:** A meets the requirement at a fraction of B's cost, and unlike B it can be undone cheaply.

## 5. Failure mode, tripwire and flip conditions
- **Failure mode:**
  - At 10x scale, the marketing build and the app build drift apart in design tokens and navigation.
  - Content editors may need preview or fast publishing that static builds don't give them.
- **Tripwires:** revisit this if any of these happens.
  - Marketing grows past about 50 pages, or has more than one editor.
  - It needs per-request personalization or ISR-style freshness.
  - Duplicated header, footer or token code needs changes in both builds more than twice a quarter.
- **Assumptions that flip the decision:**
  - If marketing and app routes are interleaved, for example logged-in users see SEO-relevant public content on the same URLs, move to B, or to Next.js for marketing only.
  - If marketing is CMS-driven with bounded staleness, use Next.js with ISR for the marketing site alone, not the app.
  - If the app already has public, indexable data routes such as listings or profiles, B becomes the likely answer.
- **Tradeoff note:**
  - *Solves:* indexable HTML for marketing.
  - *Costs:* a second build target and a shared-token discipline.
  - *Not when:* SEO-relevant content depends on app data or per-user rendering.
  - *Misuse breaks:* marketing pages quietly import app state and ship the whole SPA bundle anyway.

## 6. Decision note (`proposed`, owner has not accepted)
```md
# Prerender marketing routes; keep SPA for the app
Context: Marketing pages need indexable HTML; app routes are private. All facts assumed, unverified.
Decision: Static/prerendered marketing (same domain), Vite SPA unchanged; no Next.js migration.
Alternatives rejected: Full Next.js migration (est. 15-40 team-days, new runtime, hard to undo); defer (fails the SEO gate).
Consequences: Two build targets; shared design tokens; revisit if marketing >50 pages, needs ISR/personalization, or duplication recurs.
```

This recommendation doesn't authorize any migration or build change. Before the owner accepts it, they should confirm the page count, whether a CMS is involved, and whether any public route depends on app data. Those answers decide between A, Next.js for marketing only, and B.
